x.author: Dan Shipper
x.role: ceo @every | the only subscription you need to stay at the edge of AI
x.summary: Every CEO Dan Shipper 探讨了 AI 时代团队协作的本质。他认为，尽管 AI 在 GDPval 基准测试中表现惊人，但 AI 的价值不在于替代人类，而在于通过个人的独特视角与责任感，将 AI 的通用输出转化为具有实际意义的洞察。
x.translation:
我审视自己在工作间隙利用 Fable 5.2 完成的任务，心想：这在过去需要五个人和 20 万美元的投入。随后我观察了团队利用同样的 AI 所做的工作。上周，在会议间隙，我分析了客户调查、制作了一款团队游戏、发现了向团队销售 Every 的机会、构建了一个 CRM 并开始进行外联。看到这些，你可能会问：我还需要团队吗？

图表似乎给出了答案。在 OpenAI 的 GDPval 基准测试中，AI 击败人类专家的比例从 2024 年的 12.4% 跃升至 2026 年的约 83%。这是对未来工作的一种宏观视角：收集大量数据并推演趋势线。但宏观视角会忽略细节。要看清真相，必须深入微观：聚焦于一个充满混乱的真实场景，并从中进行推演。

我们让 Every 的每个人都能访问同样的客户调查和 AI 模型。
• 我发现了向团队销售的机会。
• Yash 发现首次订阅者流失是因为我们发送了过多的邮件。
• Dan 发现许多读者感到孤独：他们对 AI 感到兴奋，但周围的人却觉得他们疯了。
• Jack 将结果变成了一个粘土动画游戏节目。

你能让 Claude 生成他们每个人发现的东西吗？也许可以。但生成可能性很廉价，知道哪些重要才难。

Matt 运行了一个实验来预测我在 Slack 中会说什么。当 Claude 尝试 400 次时，它有 93% 的概率生成类似我的回答。但当它需要对自己的回答进行排序时，我的回答只有约 60% 的概率进入前 10%。

团队中的每个人都负责世界不同的部分。这种责任感缩小了他们的关注范围，而他们的视角帮助他们决定什么重要到值得采取行动。团队比单一的默认提示词探索了更多的可能性，并能为所发现的结果负责。

显而易见的反对意见是：模型在排序方面会变得更好。我认为确实如此。但当这种情况发生时，人不会停滞不前。将 2026 年的 Yash 与 2027 年的 Claude 进行比较，忽略了 2027 年的 Yash 也会进步，他将拥有多一年的经验，并使用 2027 年的 Claude。

随着模型的改进和普及，它们提高了所有人的基准线。默认答案成了基础，真正的价值在于利用你的视角和责任感去超越它。

这就是为什么我认为我们需要改变衡量 AI 的方式。与其只问模型在公认的问题上表现如何，不如问：从我的视角出发，它在处理我的工作时表现如何？

宏观视角能向我们展示能力曲线，而微观视角能帮助我们看清在驾驭这一曲线时，我们可以构建什么，以及我们将成为什么样的人。
x.recommendation: 本文深刻反思了 AI 时代“个人 vs 团队”的价值悖论。对于 AI 从业者而言，它提供了一个核心启示：AI 虽能拉平能力基准线，但无法替代人类基于特定责任和独特视角所做的决策与判断。这是理解未来人机协作模式的必读之作。

rawTweets.text:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

x.summary: 前Dropbox CTO Aditya Agarwal 深度剖析了当前AI创业的两大范式：一是将AI融入工作流的“AI扩散型”SaaS，二是利用AI加速科学发现的“AI前沿型”硬科技。他明确指出，后者虽被外界低估，却是未来模型驱动回报的核心增长点。
x.translation:
目前创业主要分为两类：

1. AI扩散（Diffusion of AI）：这相当于当代的“垂直SaaS”。虽然有多种落地模式（如FDE公司、整合型或横向产品），但核心逻辑一致：将AI部署在最贴近实际工作场景的地方。Profound、Cognition、Harvey等公司均属此类，未来将涌现大量优秀企业。

2. AI前沿（Frontier of AI）：这是最具看点的领域。利用AI加速科学进步，再基于这些突破构建产品。这一类别门槛较高，但我们在SPC看到了很多案例：
- Externa：通过为蛋白质增加数百种新的化学构件，实现针对疾病的定制化药物设计，而非受限于自然界现有的结构。
- Epana Bio：利用基因组学与AI设计针对疾病细胞起源的自身免疫疗法。
- VenomicsAI：利用AI加速毒液药物研发。
- Equivariant：为半导体行业提供多物理场建模。

（当然，AI基础设施类公司也一直存在，该领域同样有许多出色的企业。）

第二类目前在外部讨论较少且认知不足，但我认为这才是未来绝大多数模型驱动回报的来源，值得更多关注。
x.recommendation: Aditya Agarwal 提供了极具战略高度的行业分类框架，帮助从业者跳出单纯的“套壳”思维。对于寻求差异化竞争优势的AI创业者和投资人，关注“AI+科学”的前沿交叉领域是捕捉下一波高壁垒红利的必修课。

It has been such a pleasure to partner with Rox from the earliest days.

I have also learnt a lot about what it means to run a company at AI-pace from @ishanmkh. His talk at our recent founder retreat was incredible. https://t.co/UdZlqzZetx

There are basically two kinds of companies to build right now.

1. Diffusion of AI
This is the "vertical SaaS" of today. There are a bunch of different models for it (FDE company, rollup, horizontal product) but ultimately it all boils down to the same thing: get AI diffused very close to where the work is being done.

Profound, Cognition, Harvey etc. A lot of great companies will get built here.

2. Frontier of AI
This is where the really interesting action is. Use AI to accelerate scientific progress, then build products from that progress.

It is a harder category to see. But we are seeing a lot more of it at @spc:

- Externa is adding hundreds of new chemical building blocks to proteins, so you can engineer a drug to match the disease instead of settling for what nature gave you.

- Epana Bio is using genomics and AI to design autoimmune therapies that go after the cellular origin of the disease.

- VenomicsAI is doing AI-accelerated drug discovery from venoms.

- Equivariant is doing multi-physics modeling for the semiconductor industry.

(There are always picks-and-shovels for AI as well. Lots of amazing companies in that category.)

Category 2 is not well understood or much talked about externally. It should be because I think that is where the vast majority of model driven returns will come from.

I wrote this article in 2024 where I wrote, you won't be judged on how much you know, but instead on how well you can allocate and manage the resources to get work done, the resources of intelligence.

You'll be allocating work to AI models and making sure the work gets done well.

And there are some really, really interesting implications if you believe this.

We're gonna be allocating work to models, and the default capability is distributed to everyone, so the responsibility and the perspective that you bring to the model is the thing that's valuable.

The first thing is, the first interesting flip is it should flip how we measure AI.

Right now when we measure AI capabilities, we measure them based on,

Consensus, is it good at problems that we all agree are worth solving?

So like math problems are easy because we can validate them.

Program problems are easy because we can validate them.

But again, by this logic, those capabilities are now distributed.

They are no longer as valuable.

And what we should be measuring instead is how good is it at doing my work from my perspective specifically?

And this is like kind of a weird flip.

It's a weird cultural inversion because I think for all of us, we have this feeling that getting to a settled answer or being able to use a settled answer or know a settled answer is where all the value is.

Like we're thinking about math and science and computer programming where your perspective doesn't actually matter.

And my view is that stuff has become much less valuable because it's commoditized.

And now the value comes from you having a non-consensus perspective that you can use to push the model to make something that you think is good.

And if you internalize that, then you start to think of things, think of model progress not as something that's going to replace you, but something that works for you, for your ends.

And as it gets better, so do you.

I think this is why the intimate matters.

When you look at what's going on in the aggregate versus the intimate, the aggregate has to freeze you.

It has to, in order to measure model progress, it has to freeze humans in 2020 and compare it to humans in 2020.

And I think the intimate empowers you to see what you might build and who you might become.

And we have all lived that perspective today.
